newsitem.title: USA: Dollar sinks on Mr. Yen's comments.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sinks on Mr. Yen's comments.

text.p: The dollar plunged Thursday after one of Japan's most influential policy-makers, who is known in financial markets as "Mr. Yen," signalled that the U.S. currency's recovery was about to end.
In New York trading, the dollar sank to 111.55 Japanese yen from 113.95 Wednesday, and it fell to 1.5097 German marks from 1.5175 marks.

Currency markets were rattled by Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara's comments in a newspaper interview, in which he said the dollar's recovery from its sharp slide last year was about to finish.
Sakakibara was dubbed "Mr. Yen" for his role in taming the raging yen in 1995, which knocked the dollar to a post-war low of 79.75 yen in April of that year.

"The Japanese are trying to put a 115 yen top in," said Stephen Flanagan, a vice president at Credit Agricole. "You've probably got more downside, as all these yen-financed bond trades around the world are put at risk."

The Japanese official's comments fuelled market speculation that the Group of Three -- Japan, Germany and the United States -- had waited until after the U.S. elections to hint that their consensus for a strong dollar was breaking down.

Traders also feared that if the Clinton administration does not quickly reaffirm its long-standing preference for a "strong" dollar, the market will probably decide that the dollar has reached its top for the year against the yen.

Dealers viewed Sakakibara's comments as particularly significant because it was the first time he has said anything negative about the dollar's rise since he became involved in driving the currency higher from its post-war low against the yen in August of 1995.
They also said Sakakibara's remarks did not imply a complete reversal of a strong dollar, but gave a signal that an excessive dollar rise was not desirable if it was not justified by fundamentals.
"We are closely watching current developments in the currency market," Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, told reporters.
Dealers said Sakakibara's comments were timely, coming right after the U.S. presidential election.

The stronger yen hurts Japanese exporters by making their products more expensive overseas, but Japanese business leaders have recently voiced concern about the rise in the dollar, as it increases the cost of materials and products they import.
